parsed_answer.content: Spring Data JDBC is designed as a lighter alternative to full-featured ORM frameworks like Hibernate and JPA. While JPA focuses on complex object-relational mapping, lazy loading, first-level caching (persistence contexts), and dirty tracking, Spring Data JDBC embraces a much simpler model: a direct, predictable bridge between database tables and immutable or mutable domain entities. It does not maintain a persistent entity identity map, nor does it perform complex cascade updates or automatic dirty checking via bytecode enhancement. Instead, it relies on aggregate roots, straightforward SQL generation via Spring's JdbcTemplate, and explicit lifecycle management. This architectural choice eliminates entire classes of ORM-induced anti-patterns, such as accidental N+1 query problems hidden behind lazy-loaded proxies, unintended flushes, and detached entity state exceptions.

items: Aggregate Roots: Spring Data JDBC enforces Domain-Driven Design (DDD) principles where an aggregate root acts as the boundary for persistence. When an aggregate is saved, the framework deletes all existing child rows belonging to that aggregate and re-inserts the current collection state, avoiding complex diff algorithms.

Relational Mapping Metadata: Instead of complex annotations like @ManyToMany, @OneToMany, and cascading strategies, Spring Data JDBC uses simpler directives like @MappedCollection and @Column, strictly mirroring foreign key relationships as simple ID references or embedded value objects.

Predictable SQL Generation: Because there is no session cache or dirty-checking mechanism, every save operation translates into deterministic, easily traceable INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE statements executed sequentially against the target relational database.

parsed_answer.content: Senior production warning: Because Spring Data JDBC handles aggregate updates by deleting all child records and re-inserting them, you must ensure that your child tables have appropriate composite primary keys or surrogate keys accompanied by efficient indexing. Failing to design your aggregate boundaries carefully can lead to unnecessary database thrashing and cascading lock contention under high-concurrency workloads.
